hero.title: Mouthguards
hero.lead: A mouthguard is worn over the upper teeth during contact sport. One made from impressions of your own teeth fits closely, stays put and is easier to talk and breathe in.

intro.heading: Custom-fitted or off the shelf?
intro.html:
Over-the-counter mouthguards come in standard sizes, or are softened in hot water and shaped by biting. A custom mouthguard is made from impressions of your own teeth, so it fits closely and is less likely to move during a hit.

A mouthguard that’s comfortable is more likely to be worn, and a well-fitted guard makes it easier to breathe, speak and drink during play.

callout.title: Book before the season starts
callout.html: A custom mouthguard needs an appointment to take impressions and time for it to be made. Children’s mouths change as they grow, so ask your dentist when theirs should be replaced.

explain.heading: What a well-fitted mouthguard helps protect against
explain.intro: No mouthguard prevents every injury, but a good one reduces the risk.
ticks: Cuts to the lips and cheeks

care.heading: Looking after your mouthguard
items: Rinse in cool water, let it air-dry, and store it in a ventilated case.
Heat can warp a mouthguard. Don’t leave it in a hot car or in the sun.
Bring it to your check-ups. Replace it if it’s damaged, loose or no longer fits, which happens often in growing children.

faqs: How long does a mouthguard last?
It depends on how often it’s used and how it’s cared for. Children usually need new ones more often as their mouths grow. Your dentist can check the fit at each visit.
Can I wear a mouthguard with braces?
Yes, but it needs to suit the braces. Talk to your dentist or orthodontist about the right option.
Is a mouthguard needed for training too?
Injuries can happen at training as well as in games, so wearing it whenever there’s a risk of contact is sensible.
cost: The cost depends on what your mouth needs, so it can only be worked out after an examination.
